newsitem.title: INDIA: U.S. balloonist begins journey home after record.
newsitem.headline: U.S. balloonist begins journey home after record.

text.p: Adventurer Steve Fossett set out on Tuesday on his long return journey to the United States, saying someone would fly around the world in a balloon within three years but declining to say if he would try himself.

After flying halfway around the world, Fossett managed to have his tattered, $300,000 balloon pulled down from a tree in a remote Indian field before leaving the landing site at Nonkhar vilage on a 13,000-km (8,000-mile) trip home.
Nonkhar is some 550 km (330 miles) southeast of the Indian capital and more than 16,000 km (10,000 miles) from St Louis, Missouri, where he began his ascent on January 13.

Martin Barnes, chief pilot of a team which flew beside Fossett in a Cessna, told Reuters at the holy Hindu city of Varanasi the team was planning to spend two more days to help Fossett recover from fatigue and collect the balloon's remains.
But Barnes said the team had only 72-hour visas, which gave them limited time to carry on their mission.
Fossett was expected to hold a news conference with U.S. ambassador Frank Wisner in Delhi on Wednesday.
It took the 52-year-old commodity broker six days, two hours and 49 minutes to reach India after taking off from the U.S..
It took another day and a half to pull down the balloon and pack the deflated bladder, propane cylinders and yellow fibreglass cabin onto two wagons pulled by tractors.
Villagers climbed up the "mahua" tree and helpers used fire brigade ladders to free the "Solo Spirit" from its branches.
Later, the equipment was to be loaded into a police truck that would move it some 150 km (95 miles) to the holy Hindu city of Varanasi, from where Fossett it will be flown back to the United States.
"I'm feeling great," a relaxed Fossett told Reuters before driving off on Tuesday, escorted by two police vehicles, for Varanasi, where he was set to spend the night before flying to Delhi.

Fossett said he was happy to have broken two ballooning records -- the greatest distance and longest time in the air -- before running short of fuel, and he called his aborted mission "a grand success."
"There are a number of competing teams to try and make it around the world and I think one of them will succeed within three years," Fossett said.

"My team has the most experience with this kind of flight. We certainly have a good chance of being the first person to do it," he earlier told Reuters outside a government guest house in nearby Sultanpur where he spent the night.
But he declined to say whether he would make a fresh bid. "I haven't made up my mind as yet, but perhaps I would," he said.
Fossett said villagers who watched in disbelief as his balloon descended onto the Ganges river plain were a great help.

"When I landed here, people looked a little apprehensive because I could not communicate with anyone as no one spoke English," he said. "But finally some more people came, to whom I could explain who I am and why I am here."
"We ran when we saw this thing hovering around this place," said 15-year-old Shiv Kumar Mishra. "Many of us thought that it was a temple sent from the heavens by the gods."
